nodes.label: Services needing ids
nodes.summary: Application services, shards and databases that create records and need unique keys.

nodes.label: ID service
nodes.summary: Generates 64-bit ids from time, machine id and sequence with no per-id coordination. Can run as a small service or be embedded in each application.

nodes.label: ID generator
nodes.summary: Composes 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch, 10 bits of machine id and 12 bits of sequence; rolls over every 4,096 ids per machine, with protection against rollover within the same millisecond.

nodes.label: Clock guard
nodes.summary: Uses NTP and refuses to generate ids if the clock runs backwards until time passes the last timestamp used.

nodes.label: Machine-id registry
nodes.summary: Assigns each worker a unique machine id at startup (Snowflake used ZooKeeper, overridable in configuration).

nodes.label: Ticket servers (Flickr)
nodes.summary: Two MySQL servers, each with a one-row table; REPLACE INTO plus LAST_INSERT_ID gives an atomic auto-increment; odd and even ids; clients round-robin.

nodes.label: UUIDv7 library
nodes.summary: Generates 128-bit ids client-side: 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp plus random bits or a counter. RFC 9562 says new systems should prefer UUIDv7 over v1.

nodes.label: Sharded database
nodes.summary: Stores records keyed by the generated ids; time-ordered ids keep index inserts local.

steps.caption: At startup the worker obtains a unique machine id.
A service asks for an id.
The generator reads the clock and checks it has not gone backwards.
The service stores the record under the id, roughly in time order.
The guard sees the current time is before the last timestamp used.
The generator waits (or fails the request) until time passes the last timestamp, rather than risking a duplicate id.
One ticket server does not respond.
The client uses the other server; ids from it keep their parity, so uniqueness holds although the two sides drift out of step.
The service creates a UUIDv7 locally.
The 128-bit id is stored; the time-ordered prefix keeps index inserts local compared with random UUIDs.
